Culture & Climate · Week 6 · Sept 8–11, 2026

Steady in a
Short Week

Week 6 is a short one. With Labor Day on Monday and staff PD on Tuesday, students return Wednesday through Friday. Short week, same standard: predictable routines, daily DBRC feedback, and timely attendance follow-up.

This week: two Morning Meeting lessons and Friday Cypher; the August 31–September 4 attendance snapshot; monthly counselor lessons for grades K–8; DBRC completion support; staff celebrations; and the updated Culture Meeting schedule.

The Commitment

It started with a shared commitment

Our shared commitments give us the language. Daily routines help students experience those commitments. When students can regulate, connect, practice, commit, and transition with support, they are better prepared to participate in a Safe, Respectful, and Responsible learning community.

Morning Meeting

The 15-Minute Neuro-Regulated Morning Circle

This week’s Morning Meeting uses the same trauma-responsive Tier 1 circle that regulates the body before instruction begins. With only two lesson days before Friday’s Cypher, each 15-minute lesson follows the same six-phase arc:

Regulate→Orient→Connect→Practice→Commit→Transition

The repeated structure gives students a predictable way to notice their internal state, use a regulation strategy, connect with others, practice a skill, name a commitment, and transition into learning.

Morning Meeting in Action

Celebrating the practice

Two August 27 clips celebrating teachers and students doing the patient work of building Morning Meeting routines. These are classroom-practice examples, not recordings of this week’s lesson sequence.

Expectations Becoming Routine

Teachers, this is strong prevention work. The routine is slowed down so students have a real chance to hear the expectation, practice it, and receive feedback. Thank you for investing this time now—clear, encouraging rehearsal is how expectations become student habits and students grow more independent.

Learning the Opening Song

Kinder teachers, this is what joyful routine-building looks like in real time. Students are learning the opening song together, joining in a little more each round, and building confidence through a predictable start. Thank you for giving our youngest learners the repetition, warmth, and celebration they need to make the routine their own.

The week’s extreme heat may have added barriers involving transportation, routines, and student wellness. Keep attendance visible each morning, follow up the same day when students are absent, and help families problem-solve barriers early.

Attendance follow-up process

Teachers should make the initial parent contact or attempt when a student begins accumulating absences. Once a student reaches five absences, the teacher should email the counseling team so counselors can follow up with the family and determine whether additional support or intervention is needed.

Early communication helps us respond before attendance concerns become more difficult to address.

DBRC

DBRC: Naming the Dip, Building the Fix

DBRC completion dropped during August 31–September 4. Daily completion matters: it gives students timely feedback and helps us identify the support they need. Tuesday’s PD focused on strengthening that daily practice together.

Because coverage is too thin for a meaningful comparison, we are not publishing a Safe/Respectful/Responsible domain breakdown—the sample is too small to be meaningful. Full domain reporting returns once completion is back where it needs to be.

Support, not a penalty

We addressed the drop directly in today’s PD training, and we want to be just as direct about what happens next: DBRC is a support system, and we are still building fidelity with it together.

Starting this week, an end-of-day email will go out for any DBRC that has not been completed. This is a reminder, not a write-up—the goal is to catch incomplete check-ins the same day, while the details are still fresh, so students get the timely feedback DBRC is built on. If you are unsure how to complete a rating or want to walk through the process together, reach out—we would rather troubleshoot with you than let a student’s data go missing.

This week’s DBRC action

Complete every assigned block as it occurs so students receive timely feedback and next week’s snapshot reflects full coverage. Use the revised rubric’s observable descriptors, involve students in understanding their ratings, and identify the next Safe, Respectful, or Responsible behavior to practice.

DBRC outcomes will continue to be reviewed alongside classroom observations, documented Tier 1 interventions, 504 implementation, and other relevant student information. The MTSS Behavior Request remains the single entry point for ongoing behavior support and DBRC consideration.

LiveSchool

Create the opportunity to earn it

LiveSchool is our schoolwide system for student incentives and rewards. Please do not routinely hand out food, candy, drinks, or other incentive items during the day simply because a student completed an assignment or met an expectation. Instead, use the item as something students can work toward through LiveSchool points:

“You can earn LiveSchool points for meeting this expectation.”
“Once you have enough points, you can use them to purchase the reward through the LiveSchool Store.”

If you already have reward items you would like students to earn, coordinate with the student’s homeroom teacher so the reward can be distributed at an appropriate time. The goal is simple: do not just give the reward—create an opportunity for students to earn it.
